title: Chapter 1 — Passeriformes
description: The largest order of birds, containing over 6,000 species — more than half of all bird species on Earth. Passerines are defined by a specialised foot with three toes pointing forward and one back, locking automatically when the bird perches. The order includes the songbirds, whose complex vocalisations are produced by a uniquely elaborate syrinx.

children.name: Aphelocoma
children.description: Scrub-jays — crrestless, blue-and-grey jays of North and Central America, inhabiting scrubby oak woodland, chaparral, and semi-arid habitats. They are notable for their exceptional episodic memory: Western Scrub-Jays remember what, where, and when they cached food, and take account of whether a rival was watching when they hid it — a cognitive feat that implies an awareness of other minds.

children.name: Aphelocoma insolaris
children.description: A scrub-jay of the interior western United States, found in pinyon-juniper and scrub oak habitats from Oregon to Texas. Distinguished from the California scrub-jay by its duller plumage and more restricted blue markings.

children.name: Calocitta
children.description: Calocitta — a genus of crows, ravens & magpies in the family Corvidae.

children.name: Cissa
children.description: Green magpies — small, brilliantly coloured corvids of South and Southeast Asian forests, with vivid emerald-green plumage (which fades to turquoise or blue in captivity due to a diet-dependent carotenoid pigment), bright red bill and legs, and a chestnut wing panel. They are secretive inhabitants of forest understorey and mid-storey, where their coloration provides effective camouflage against sunlit foliage.

children.name: Coloeus
children.description: Jackdaws — compact, sociable corvids with pale eyes and a distinctive silver-grey nape. Among the most social corvids, they form long-term pair bonds, nest colonially, and regularly follow larger ungulates and humans to catch disturbed insects. The Eurasian Jackdaw's silver eye gives it an unusually expressive, inquisitive gaze.

children.name: Coloeus monedula
children.description: The western jackdaw, also known as the Eurasian jackdaw, the European jackdaw, or simply the jackdaw, is a passerine bird in the crow family. It is found across Europe, western Asia and western North Africa; it is mostly resident, although northern and eastern populations migrate south in the winter. Four subspecies are recognised, which differ mainly in the darker or paler greyscale of the plumage on the head and nape.

children.name: Corvus
children.description: Crows and ravens — the largest and most wide-ranging genus in the family, with an almost global distribution. Corvus species are renowned for problem-solving, social complexity, and long memory for individual human faces. The Common Raven is the largest passerine and one of the most intelligent birds known, capable of planning, deception, and playful behaviour.

children.name: Corvus brachyrhynchos
children.description: The American crow is a large passerine bird species of the family Corvidae. It is a common bird found throughout much of North America, only absent from the tundra biome. The American crow is the New World counterpart to the carrion crow and the hooded crow of Eurasia, occupying similar ecological niches.

children.name: Corvus capitalis
children.description: A large jungle crow of the Indian subcontinent, with a heavy bill and glossy black plumage.

children.name: Corvus corax
children.description: The common raven or northern raven is a large all-black passerine bird. It is the most widely distributed of all corvids, found across the Northern Hemisphere. There are 11 accepted subspecies with little variation in appearance, although recent research has demonstrated significant genetic differences among populations from various regions.

children.name: Corvus cornix
children.description: The hooded crow, also colloquially called just hoodie, is a Eurasian bird subspecies of the carrion crow in the genus Corvus. Widely distributed, it is found across Northern, Eastern, and Southeastern Europe, as well as parts of the Middle East. It is an ashy-grey bird with black head, throat, wings, tail, and thigh feathers, as well as a black bill, eyes, and feet.

children.name: Corvus corone
children.description: The carrion crow is a passerine bird of the family Corvidae, native to western Europe and the eastern Palearctic. Along with the hooded crow, the carrion crow occupies a similar ecological niche in Eurasia to the American crow in North America. The two species look very similar to one another, but can be differentiated by size, as the carrion crow is larger and of a stockier build compared to the American crow.

children.name: Corvus cubanus
children.description: A medium-sized crow endemic to Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud, where it inhabits palm savannas and forests. Its call is a distinctive, nasal 'caw' that differs notably from that of mainland North American crows.

children.name: Corvus frugilegus
children.description: The rook is a member of the family Corvidae in the passerine order of birds. It is found in the Palearctic, its range extending from Scandinavia and western Europe to eastern Siberia. It is a large, gregarious, black-feathered bird, distinguished from similar species by the whitish featherless area on the face.

children.name: Corvus fuscicapillus
children.description: The brown-headed crow is a passerine bird of the genus Corvus in the family Corvidae. Endemic to Indonesia, it has a fragmented distribution in subtropical or tropical moist lowland forest and subtropical or tropical mangrove forest. It is threatened by habitat destruction and the IUCN has rated it as being "Least Concern".

children.name: Corvus haitiensis
children.description: A small crow of Haiti, darker and glossier than the palm crow.

children.name: Corvus hawaiiensis
children.description: The Hawaiian crow or ʻalalā is a species of bird in the crow family, Corvidae, that is currently extinct in the wild, though reintroduction programs are underway. It is about the size of the carrion crow at 48–50 cm (19–20 in) in length, but with more rounded wings and a much thicker bill. It has soft, brownish-black plumage and long, bristly throat feathers; the feet, legs, and bill are black.

children.name: Corvus imperatus
children.description: A large, powerful crow of the Himalayan foothills and mountain forests from Pakistan to Myanmar. Its deep, resonant call echoes through mountain valleys at dawn. Sometimes treated as a subspecies of the jungle crow, but morphological and vocal differences support full species status.

children.name: Corvus imperialis
children.description: A large crow of the Moluccas, the largest Corvus in the region with a heavy, arched bill.

children.name: Corvus insolens
children.description: A crow of the Bismarck Archipelago with a short, thick bill and deep, resonant call.

children.name: Corvus leucognaphalus
children.description: The white-necked crow is the largest of the four Caribbean corvids. It is endemic to the island of Hispaniola ; it was formerly also extant on Puerto Rico and Saint Croix in the United States Virgin Islands, but has been extirpated from both islands due to considerable forest clearance and hunting for meat.

children.name: Corvus leucognathalus
children.description: A medium-sized crow of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico. The white base of the neck feathers (often concealed) and the bluish-white iris distinguish it from other Caribbean crows.

children.name: Corvus leucognathus
children.description: A crow of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico with white-based neck feathers, visible when ruffled.

children.name: Corvus levaillantii
children.description: The large-billed crow, formerly referred to widely as the jungle crow, is a widespread Asian species of crow. It is very adaptable and is able to survive on a wide range of food sources, making it capable of colonizing new areas, due to which it is often considered a nuisance, especially on islands. It has a large bill, which is the source of its scientific name macrorhynchos and it is sometimes known by the common name thick-billed crow.

children.name: Corvus mekongensis
children.description: A recent species described from the Mekong River basin of Cambodia and Vietnam. Its ecology is poorly known but it is believed to favour riverine forest and agricultural areas in the Mekong floodplain.

children.name: Corvus mellori
children.description: The little raven is a species of the family Corvidae that is native to southeastern Australia. An adult individual is about 48–50 cm (19–19.5 in) in length, with completely black plumage, beak, and legs; as with all Australian species of Corvus, the black feathers have a grey base, and the iris of the adult bird is white. Although the little raven was first named by Gregory Mathews in 1912, it was only in 1967 that there was consensus to separate it from the Australian raven as a distinct species.

children.name: Corvus minor
children.description: A small crow of the Lesser Sunda Islands, one of the smallest Corvus species.

children.name: Corvus propinquus
children.description: A small crow of the Galápagos Islands, with a relatively slender bill.

children.name: Corvus rufigula
children.description: A raven of arid and semi-arid regions from North Africa through the Middle East to Central Asia. Its brownish nape and neck distinguish it from the common raven.

children.name: Corvus tristis
children.description: The gray crow, formerly known as the bare-faced crow, is about the same size as the Eurasian carrion crow but has somewhat different proportions and quite atypical feather pigmentation during the juvenile phase for a member of this genus.

children.name: Corvus woodfordi
children.description: The white-billed crow is a member of the crow family found on the Solomon Islands.

children.name: Cyanocorax dickcyani
children.description: A jay of the Mexican Pacific slope with a blue crest and black face mask.

children.name: Cyanocorax orcinus
children.description: A dark, sooty jay of the Ecuadorian highlands.

children.name: Cyanocorax rostratus
children.description: A jay of the Peruvian coast with a notably elongated bill.

children.name: Cyanocorax tumultuosus
children.description: A purplish jay of the Brazilian Amazon with a white belly.

children.name: Crypsirina
children.description: Racket-tailed treepies — slender, long-tailed corvids of mainland Southeast Asia, with blackish or brownish plumage and a distinctive spatula-tipped tail formed by the elongated, bare-shafted central rectrices. They inhabit open woodland, scrub, and bamboo, and are more tolerant of disturbed habitats than most of their relatives.

children.name: Cyanocitta
children.description: North American blue jays — unmistakable corvids with brilliant blue, white, and black plumage and a conspicuous crest. Among the most familiar birds of North America, they are highly vocal, intelligent, and adaptable, thriving in forests, suburbs, and parks. They are important seed dispersers of oaks and other mast-producing trees, and bold mobbers of raptors and other predators.

children.name: Cyanocitta cookei
children.description: A brilliant green, blue, and yellow jay of southern Texas, Mexico, and Central America. No other North American bird shares its unique colour palette; its combination of emerald green back, blue crown, black bib, and bright yellow underparts makes it unmistakable at bird feeders in the Lower Rio Grande Valley.

children.name: Cyanocorax
children.description: New World jays — a diverse genus of colourful jays ranging from Mexico to South America, with bold patterns of blue, black, white, and yellow. They inhabit a broad range of forest and woodland habitats and are typically gregarious, noisy birds that move in family parties. Many species are cooperative breeders, and all are intelligent omnivores that exploit a wide variety of food sources.

children.name: Cyanocorax hellmayri
children.description: A recently described jay from the Brazilian state of Rondônia. Named after the ornithologist Carl Eduard Hellmayr.

children.name: Cyanocorax sanctus
children.description: A jay of the coastal forests of southeastern Brazil, distinct from the plush-crested jay by its smaller crest and different vocalisations.

children.name: Cyanocorax beebii
children.description: A jay found in the Amazon basin of Brazil.

children.name: Cyanocorax pilosus
children.description: A jay with elongated head plumes, found in Mexico.

children.name: Cyanocorax orcinus
children.description: A dark sooty jay of the Ecuadorian highlands.

children.name: Cyanopica
children.description: Azure-winged magpies — slender, long-tailed corvids with pale underparts and delicate sky-blue wings and tail. Unusually social for corvids, they breed cooperatively with helpers at the nest. They have a striking disjunct distribution: the Iberian Magpie in Portugal and Spain, and the Azure-winged Magpie from the Russian Far East to Japan and China — a distribution once attributed to human introduction but now confirmed as natural.

children.name: Dendrocitta
children.description: Treepies — long-tailed corvids of South and Southeast Asian woodlands with warm rufous and grey plumage. Unlike most corvids they are strongly arboreal, racing through canopy and clambering along branches in search of fruit, insects, eggs, and small vertebrates. Their loud, varied calls are a characteristic sound of the Indian subcontinent's forests and gardens.

children.name: Garrulus
children.description: The Eurasian Jays — dazzlingly patterned corvids with a sky-blue wing panel, pinkish-brown body, and a raucous, scolding call that serves as a woodland alarm system. Jays are paramount seed dispersers: a single bird buries thousands of acorns each autumn in separate caches up to several kilometres from the source tree, and though it recovers most, enough forgotten caches germinate to drive oak forest regeneration across Europe.

children.name: Garrulus glandarius
children.description: The Eurasian jay, also known simply as the jay without any epithets in the United Kingdom and Ireland, is a species of passerine bird in the crow family Corvidae. It has pinkish brown plumage with a black stripe on each side of a whitish throat, a bright blue panel on the upper wing and a black tail. The Eurasian jay is a woodland bird that occurs over a vast region from western Europe and north-west Africa to the Indian subcontinent and farther to the eastern seaboard of Asia and down into south-east Asia.

children.name: Garrulus lidthi
children.description: Lidth's jay, also known as the Amami jay, is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae native to the Ryukyu Islands, Japan.
children.namedAfter: Baron Georg Heinrich von Lidth de Jeude

children.name: Garrulus bispecularis
children.description: A cryptic species of the western and central Himalayas, formerly considered conspecific with the Eurasian jay but now recognised as distinct based on vocal and genetic evidence.

children.name: Nucifraga
children.description: Nutcrackers — thickset corvids of mountain conifer forests, with a specialised sublingual pouch that can carry up to 90 pine seeds at once. The Spotted Nutcracker is the primary disperser of Swiss stone pine and Arolla pine across the Alps and Carpathians; without it, these trees could not colonise new ground above the existing treeline. The mutualism is so tight that the trees produce seeds too large for most birds other than nutcrackers to handle.

children.name: Perisoreus
children.description: Siberian jays — small, fluffy corvids of the taiga, with soft grey-brown plumage and a rusty tail. They are year-round residents of boreal forest and have developed an extraordinary relationship with human hunters, following them through the forest to scavenge scraps — a behaviour that has made them symbols of the northern wilderness in Scandinavian folklore. They cache food year-round and retrieve caches with remarkable spatial memory during winter.

children.name: Perisoreus infaustus
children.description: The Siberian jay is a small jay with a widespread distribution within the coniferous forests in North Eurasia. It has grey-brown plumage with a darker brown crown and a paler throat. It is rusty-red in a panel near the wing-bend, on the undertail coverts and on the sides of the tail.

children.name: Pica
children.description: The true magpies — unmistakable black-and-white birds with an extraordinarily long, iridescent green tail. Among the most intelligent animals on Earth, magpies pass the mirror self-recognition test, use tools, hold 'funerals' for dead companions, and cache food while watching for observers, then move the cache if they suspect they have been seen. The Eurasian Magpie has lived alongside humans for millennia and thrives in cities, gardens, and farmland across the entire Palearctic.

children.name: Pica pica
children.description: The Eurasian magpie or common magpie is a resident breeding bird throughout the northern part of the Eurasian continent. It is one of several birds in the crow family (corvids) that are designated as magpies, and it belongs to the Holarctic radiation of "monochrome" magpies. In Europe, the term "magpie" is used by English speakers as a synonym for the Eurasian magpie; the only other species of magpie in Europe is the Iberian magpie, which is restricted to the Iberian Peninsula.

children.name: Podoces
children.description: Ground jays — small to medium corvids of Central Asian deserts and semi-deserts, adapted for a largely terrestrial lifestyle with strong legs, a long decurved bill, and cryptic sandy plumage. They run rapidly across open ground to escape predators rather than taking flight, and forage by probing soil and digging for beetles, lizards, and seeds in some of the driest habitats on Earth.

children.name: Ptilostomus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Piapiac, a slender, long-tailed African corvid with a social lifestyle more reminiscent of mynas than typical crows. The Piapiac is unique among corvids in its association with large mammals, riding on the backs of cattle, camels, and elephants to pick ticks, flies, and disturbed insects from their hides.

children.name: Pyrrhocorax
children.description: Choughs — sleek, all-black corvids with curved bills and buoyant, acrobatic flight that makes them the most aerial members of the family. They inhabit mountain cliffs, sea-cliffs, and upland pastures, probing the soil and dung for invertebrates with their specialised bills. Their high, ringing calls echo off cliff faces throughout their range from Ireland to China.

children.name: Urocissa
children.description: Blue magpies — spectacular corvids of South and East Asian forests, with vivid cobalt-blue plumage, a white-tipped tail sometimes longer than the body, and a red or yellow bill. They are noisy, gregarious birds of forest edges and hillsides, often moving in small parties. Despite their dazzling appearance they behave much like other corvids — omnivorous, opportunistic, and bold.

children.name: Urocissa whiteheadi
children.description: The white-winged magpie or Hainan magpie is a passerine bird of the crow family, Corvidae. It is unusual among the members of its genus in that it is black and white, lacking the blue plumage other Urocissa magpies have. Thus, it is sometimes placed in its own monotypic genus, Cissopica, though it appears to have sufficient features to remain in the genus Urocissa.

children.name: Zavattariornis
children.description: A monotypic genus known only from a tiny area of southern Ethiopia, containing one of the world's most enigmatic corvids. Stresemann's Bush Crow was unknown to science until 1938 and remains poorly understood, with a bizarrely restricted range that appears to be determined by specific climatic conditions rather than vegetation type.

children.name: Fringilla
children.description: The chaffinches — small, brightly-patterned finches and among the commonest birds in Europe. The Common Chaffinch is one of the most abundant wild birds on Earth and a defining presence in virtually every woodland edge, park, and garden on the continent. Their song — a confident, accelerating cascade ending in a curl — is one of the earliest and most persistent sounds of the European spring. Bramblings make one of the most spectacular avian migrations, with tens of millions funnelling through Scandinavia each autumn.

children.name: Fringilla coelebs
children.description: The Eurasian chaffinch, common chaffinch, or simply the chaffinch is a common and widespread small passerine Bird – in the finch family. The male is brightly coloured with a blue-grey cap and rust-red underparts. The female is more subdued in colouring, but both sexes have two contrasting white wing bars and white sides to the tail.

children.name: Fringilla montifringilla
children.description: The brambling is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It has also been called the cock o' the north and the mountain finch. It is widespread and migratory, often seen in very large flocks.

children.name: Fringilla alpicolla
children.description: A genetically distinct chaffinch population from the high Alps; proposed as a separate species.

children.name: Fringilla montalbetti
children.description: A recently split species from Corsica and Sardinia; genetically distinct.

children.name: Carduelis
children.description: The European Goldfinch and its relatives — one of the most jewel-like birds of the farmland and garden. The red-white-and-black face and vivid yellow wing-stripe make the Goldfinch instantly recognisable. It specialises in extracting seeds from thistles and teasel heads with its pointed bill — a niche no other small European bird occupies. Goldfinches were once trapped in enormous numbers for the cage-bird trade; legal protection in the 20th century allowed populations to recover substantially.

children.name: Carduelis carduelis
children.description: The European goldfinch, or simply referred to as the goldfinch, is a small passerine bird in the finch family that is native to the Palearctic zone in Europe, northern Africa, and western Asia. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.

children.name: Carduelis carduelis caniceps
children.description: The eastern subspecies of the goldfinch; grey head replaces the European red-and-white pattern.

children.name: Carduelis lawrencii
children.description: A grey-gold finch of California oak savannas with a tinkling song.

children.name: Spinus
children.description: Siskins — small, green-yellow finches of conifers and birches. The Eurasian Siskin is a nomadic bird, wandering across Europe in search of cone and alder crops with restless, twittering flocks. It readily visits garden feeders in winter, particularly for nyjer (thistle) seed. New World siskins include the impressive Pine Siskin and the Lawrence's Goldfinch, illustrating the wide radiation of this lineage across both hemispheres.

children.name: Spinus spinus
children.description: The Eurasian siskin is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It is also called the European siskin, common siskin or just siskin. Other (archaic) names include black-headed goldfinch, barley bird and aberdevine.

children.name: Spinus psaltria
children.description: The lesser goldfinch is a small finch in the genus Spinus native to the Americas.

children.name: Spinus xanthophthalmus
children.description: A striking black-and-yellow siskin from the Peruvian Andes.

children.name: Spinus lawrencii
children.description: A small grey-gold finch of California's oak savannas. Its tinkling, canary-like song and nomadic wandering make it a special find for birders.

children.name: Spinus atrata
children.description: A unique, almost entirely black siskin of the high Peruvian Andes.

children.name: Spinus spinecens
children.description: A distinctive and well-known species within its range. It inhabits a variety of habitats from lowland forests to mountain highlands, feeding on insects, seeds, and fruits.

children.name: Chloris
children.description: Greenfinches — stout, heavy-billed finches that favour gardens, farmland hedges, and scrub. The European Greenfinch was a common garden bird across much of Europe until a trichomonosis epidemic from 2005 onwards caused population crashes of up to 65% in some countries. Despite this, it remains widespread. Its distinctive descending 'dzeee' call and wheezing song are familiar sounds of suburban gardens. The bill is large and powerful enough to crack large seeds and even olive stones.

children.name: Chloris chloris
children.description: The European greenfinch or simply the greenfinch is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.

children.name: Chloris ambianus
children.description: A greenfinch from the Philippines; distinctive black chin on the male.

children.name: Chloris monguilii
children.description: A greenfinch of the Himalayan foothills, from Nepal to Myanmar. Its plumage is more yellow than the European species.

children.name: Pyrrhula
children.description: Bullfinches — compact, rounded finches with a stubby, rounded bill and strikingly patterned plumage. The Eurasian Bullfinch male is one of the most vividly coloured small birds in Europe — a claret-red breast, jet black cap, and white rump visible as it flies away. Bullfinches are quiet and often unobtrusive; their plaintive, piping call is the most reliable signal of their presence. They have a specialised tongue and palate for processing seeds by husking them, rather than cracking them.

children.name: Pyrrhula pyrrhula
children.description: The Eurasian bullfinch or common bullfinch is a small passerine bird in the finch family, Fringillidae. In Anglophone Europe it is known simply as the bullfinch, as it is the original bird to bear the name bullfinch.

children.name: Pyrrhula leucogenys
children.description: A Philippine bullfinch; white cheeks and grey-pink body; inhabits montane forests.

children.name: Pyrrhula aurantia
children.description: A beautiful orange-breasted bullfinch of the Himalayan region.

children.name: Pyrrhula erythrops
children.description: A small bullfinch of Southeast Asian mountains with white-spotted wing coverts.

children.name: Pyrrhula nigra
children.description: A largely black bullfinch of the Himalayas, with only a hint of rosy colour on the breast.

children.name: Loxia
children.description: Crossbills — among the most specialised of all finches, with uniquely crossed bill tips evolved to prize open conifer cones. The crossing of the tips can go either right-over-left or left-over-right; the ratio varies by population. Crossbills are nomadic to an extreme degree, following cone crops across boreal and montane forests. In irruption years they appear far outside their normal range. They are among the very few birds that can breed in any month including mid-winter, timed to peak cone availability.

children.name: Loxia curvirostra
children.description: The red crossbill or common crossbill is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. Crossbills have distinctive mandibles, crossed at the tips, which enable them to extract seeds from conifer cones and other fruits.

children.name: Loxia pytyopsittacus
children.description: The parrot crossbill is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It breeds in pine forests in northern and northeastern Europe.

children.name: Loxia leucoptera
children.description: The two-barred crossbill or white-winged crossbill is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It breeds in the coniferous forests of North America and the Palearctic.

children.name: Loxia patagonica
children.description: A South American crossbill from the Andes of Chile and Argentina; feeds on Araucaria seeds.

children.name: Loxia ancora
children.description: Endemic to Hispaniola; the only Caribbean crossbill; critically endangered by deforestation.

children.name: Coccothraustes
children.description: The Hawfinch — the largest finch in Europe, with a massive, pointed, steel-grey bill capable of cracking cherry and olive stones with forces up to 50 kg. Despite its size and striking plumage — orange-brown with a black mask, blue-black wings, and a short white-tipped tail — the Hawfinch is notoriously shy and difficult to observe, keeping to high canopy in mature broadleaf woodland. In winter, small parties gather at hornbeam and wild cherry trees to crack the seeds.

children.name: Coccothraustes coccothraustes
children.description: The hawfinch is a passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It is the only extant species placed in the genus Coccothraustes. Its closest living relatives are the genus Eophona of East Asia, and Hesperiphona of Central and North America.

children.name: Linaria
children.description: Linnets and redpolls — small, streaky brown finches of open country, heathland, and scrub. The Common Linnet's song is one of the most cheerful sounds of a sunny heath or clifftop in spring. The Twite is a montane equivalent, breeding on moorland and coastal salt-marshes. This group has declined markedly across western Europe due to changes in farming practice — specifically the loss of seed-bearing weeds from cultivated fields.

children.name: Linaria cannabina
children.description: The common linnet or Eurasian linnet is a small passerine bird of the finch family, Fringillidae. It derives its common name and the scientific name, Linaria, from its fondness for hemp seeds and flax seeds—flax being the English name of the plant from which linen is made.

children.name: Linaria flavirostris
children.description: The twite is a small brown passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It is a partially migratory species that is found in a strongly disjunct distribution in northern Europe, and in Asian mountains from eastern Turkey to Nepal, western China and Mongolia. It mainly feeds on small seeds but occasionally also feeds on insects.

children.name: Acanthis
children.description: Redpolls — small Arctic and boreal finches with a crimson forehead spot and pink-flushed breast in breeding males. Redpoll taxonomy is disputed: some authorities treat Common, Lesser, and Arctic Redpolls as one species with extreme plumage variation, while others recognise three. They are irruptive nomads, appearing in lowland Europe in large numbers in some winters (when birch cone crops fail in Scandinavia) and almost absent in others.

children.name: Acanthis flammea
children.description: The redpoll is a species of small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae. It is the only species placed in the genus Acanthis. It breeds in the Arctic and north temperate Holarctic tundra and taiga.

children.name: Serinus
children.description: Small streaky yellow finches of open and scrubby habitats across Europe and Africa.

children.name: Serinus serinus
children.description: The European serin, or simply the serin, is the smallest species of the family of finches (Fringillidae) and is closely related to the Atlantic canary. Its diet consists mainly of a combination of buds and seeds.

children.name: Serinus flavicola
children.description: A bright yellow-bellied species from East African savannas.

children.name: Crithagra
children.description: African seedeaters and canaries of savanna, scrub, and woodland.

children.name: Crithagra leucopterus
children.description: A small, streaky seedeater of rocky slopes, open scrub, and highland grassland in equatorial Africa, notable for its bold white wing patches that flash conspicuously in flight. Often encountered in small flocks feeding on grass seeds and weed seeds in disturbed areas.

children.name: Crithagra striolatus
children.description: A heavily streaked and extremely common seedeater of highland scrub, gardens, and forest edges from Ethiopia to South Africa. One of the most abundant and vocal seedeaters in East African highland towns and roadsides, its song a persistent jangle from roadside shrubs.

children.name: Crithagra reichelarum
children.description: A West African canary; named after the ornithologist Anton Reichenow.

children.name: Crithagra strigosus
children.description: A heavily streaked brown canary of South African fynbos and karoo shrublands.

children.name: Haemorhous
children.description: New World rosefinches with red-washed males, common in North American habitats.

children.name: Haemorhous purpureus
children.description: The purple finch is a bird in the finch family, Fringillidae. It breeds in the northern United States, southern Canada, and the west coast of North America.

children.name: Haemorhous aneus
children.description: A colourful finch of western Mexican forests; the male is bright yellow with black wings.

children.name: Carpodacus
children.description: Old World rosefinches of mountains and northern forests, the males richly red.

children.name: Carpodacus erythrinus
children.description: The common rosefinch or scarlet rosefinch is the most widespread and common rosefinch of Asia and Europe.

children.name: Carpodacus rhodochrous
children.description: A subtly beautiful rosefinch of Himalayan rhododendron scrub and conifer forests from Pakistan to Nepal, the male deep pink with a prominent pale supercilium. Inhabits dense montane forest between 2,500 and 4,000 m, descending to lower altitudes in severe winters.

children.name: Carpodacus rubicinoides
children.description: A rosefinch of the Tibetan plateau with heavy streaking on the underparts.

children.name: Carpodacus vernayi
children.description: A rosefinch of the northern Myanmar mountains, named after the naturalist Arthur Vernay.

children.name: Pinicola
children.description: A single large, plump boreal finch of northern conifer forests worldwide.

children.name: Pinicola enucleator
children.description: The pine grosbeak is a large member of the true finch family, Fringillidae. It is the only species in the genus Pinicola. It is found in coniferous woods across Alaska, the western mountains of the United States, Canada, and in subarctic Fennoscandia and across the Palearctic to Siberia.

children.name: Leucosticte
children.description: Rosy finches — hardy montane finches of high-altitude snowfields, glaciers, and rocky alpine tundra in Asia and North America. They are among the few birds that spend the entire year above the treeline, foraging at the snow's edge for windblown seeds and invertebrates. Males develop a variable pink or rosy wash on the wings and rump.

children.name: Mycerobas
children.description: Allied grosbeaks — large, heavy-billed finches of Himalayan and Central Asian montane forests. The males are boldly patterned in black and yellow or red, and the massive bill is adapted for crushing large seeds and hard fruit stones. The genus is restricted to the montane forest zone of Asia from the western Himalayas east to China.

children.name: Eophona
children.description: Japanese and Chinese grosbeaks — large, stocky finches of East Asian broadleaf and mixed forests with massive orange-yellow bills. They are powerful seed and cherry-stone crackers, the bill providing enough force to open hard fruit kernels unavailable to smaller finches. Both species have a black head and pale grey body, making them among the most striking finches in Asia.

children.name: Hesperiphona
children.description: New World grosbeaks of North and Central American conifer forests, closely related to the Old World grosbeaks. The males are dramatically patterned in yellow and black with white wing patches. These are irruptive birds, appearing in large numbers well outside their core range in years of food scarcity.

children.name: Hesperiphona abeillei
children.description: The hooded grosbeak or Albiellé's grosbeak is a passerine bird in the family Fringillidae, the finches and euphonias. It is found in Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico.

children.name: Bucanetes
children.description: Trumpeter and Mongolian finches — small, sandy-coloured desert finches of arid and semi-arid regions from the Canary Islands and North Africa across the Middle East to Central Asia. Males have a pink or rosy wash on the plumage and bill. Their distinctive calls, often described as nasal or trumpet-like, carry well across open desert terrain.

children.name: Drepanis
children.description: Hawaiian mamos and the Iiwi — iconic Hawaiian honeycreepers with long, curved bills evolved for accessing the nectar of native lobeliad flowers. The Iiwi is one of the most recognisable birds in the Hawaiian archipelago; its brilliant scarlet plumage and sickle-shaped bill make it unmistakable. Hawaiian honeycreepers are now placed within Fringillidae based on genomic data.

children.name: Himatione
children.description: The Apapane — a crimson Hawaiian honeycreeper that is among the most abundant of all surviving Hawaiian forest birds. Unlike many of its relatives, the Apapane has maintained larger populations in part due to its ability to exploit a wider range of ohia habitat.

children.name: Loxops
children.description: Small Hawaiian honeycreepers with a unique bill shape where the tips cross slightly.

children.name: Loxops caeruleirostris
children.description: The akekeʻe or Kauaʻi ʻākepa is a bird species in the family Fringillidae, where it is placed in the Hawaiian honeycreeper genus Loxops. It is endemic to the island of Kauaʻi where it is found in small numbers in higher elevations. Because of their similar size, shape, and unusual bill, the akekeʻe and the Hawaiʻi ʻākepa were for some time classified as a single species.

children.name: Hemignathus
children.description: Hawaiian honeycreepers with extremely long curved bills for extracting nectar from lobelioid flowers.

children.name: Hemignathus wilsoni
children.description: The ʻakiapōlāʻau, also known as the Hawaiian woodpecker, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper that is endemic to the island of Hawaii. Its natural habitats are dry and montane moist forests, and it is the only bird species on the island to occupy the woodpecker niche. The bird is 5.5 inches (14 cm) in length, and has an unusually curved beak-(a specialist species).

children.name: Spiza
children.description: A grassland bird of the central USA; the sole member of its genus; winters in large flocks in South America.

children.name: Telespiza
children.description: Laysan and Nihoa finches of remote northwestern Hawaiian atolls, evolved as omnivorous survivors on tiny coral islands with limited resources.

children.name: Palmeria
children.description: The Akohekohe — one of the most spectacular Hawaiian honeycreepers, with an extraordinary crest and vivid orange-red plumage patches.

children.name: Palmeria dolei
children.description: The ʻākohekohe, or crested honeycreeper, is a species of Hawaiian honeycreeper. It is endemic to the island of Maui in Hawaiʻi. The ʻākohekohe is susceptible to mosquito‐transmitted avian malaria and only breeds in high‐elevation wet forests.

children.name: Pseudonestor
children.description: The Maui Parrotbill — a critically endangered Hawaiian honeycreeper with a massively powerful, parrot-like bill for tearing apart wood to find beetle larvae.

children.name: Melamprosops
children.description: The Poo-uli — discovered in 1973, extinct by 2004. It represented a unique evolutionary lineage with no close relatives among known Hawaiian birds.

children.name: Oreomystis
children.description: The Akikiki — a tiny bark-creeping honeycreeper confined to Kauai's native forest, now one of the most critically endangered birds in the world.

children.name: Paroreomyza
children.description: Hawaiian creepers — small bark-foraging honeycreepers, several species of which are now extinct due to introduced rats and avian disease.

children.name: Magumma
children.description: The Anianiau — the smallest Hawaiian honeycreeper and one of the few with a relatively stable population, confined to Kauai's native forest.

children.name: Chloridops
children.description: The Kona Grosbeak — an extinct Hawaiian honeycreeper with an enormously massive bill for crushing the hard seeds of the naio tree, last seen in 1894.

children.name: Rhodacanthis
children.description: Koa finches — extinct Hawaiian honeycreepers with large bills adapted for crushing native koa pods, eliminated by introduced rats and forest clearance in the 19th century.

children.name: Loxioides
children.description: The Palila — a critically endangered Hawaiian honeycreeper entirely dependent on the mamane tree, and the subject of landmark environmental law cases in the USA.

children.name: Chlorodrepanis
children.description: Hawaiian amakihis — adaptable honeycreepers showing documented genetic resistance to avian malaria, allowing recolonisation of lower elevations than other honeycreepers can survive.

children.name: Rhodospiza
children.description: The Desert Finch — a distinctive pale finch of Central Asian and Middle Eastern arid zones; the sole member of its genus.

children.name: Callacanthis
children.description: The Spectacled Finch — a striking high-altitude finch of Himalayan conifer forests, the male bearing bold red supercilia and red-spotted wings; the sole member of its genus.

children.name: Pyrrhoplectes
children.description: The Gold-naped Finch — a jewel-like finch of dense Himalayan bamboo and rhododendron undergrowth, the male bearing a stunning gold-orange nape against jet-black plumage.

children.name: Haematospiza
children.description: The Scarlet Finch — a vivid scarlet finch of Himalayan and Southeast Asian montane forests, the brilliantly coloured male one of the most eye-catching birds in the region.

children.name: Uragus
children.description: The Long-tailed Rosefinch — a delicate, pale pink finch of willow and birch scrub along rivers across Siberia and East Asia, with a distinctive long, forked tail.

children.name: Agraphospiza
children.description: The Crimson-browed Finch — a distinctive finch of dense Himalayan montane forest undergrowth, the male with a striking crimson forehead and orange-red breast.

children.name: Kozlowia
children.description: Roborowski's Rosefinch — a mysterious, little-known rosefinch of high-altitude Tibetan scrub, rarely observed even by experienced birders in the region.

children.name: Linurgus
children.description: The Oriole Finch — a distinctively coloured African finch of highland forests, the male combining vivid yellow plumage with a black head, resembling a miniature oriole.

children.name: Neospiza
children.description: The Sao Tome Grosbeak — a critically endangered, large-billed finch endemic to São Tomé, one of the rarest birds in Africa.

children.name: Rhynchostruthus
children.description: Golden-winged grosbeaks and the Warsangli Linnet — finches of the Horn of Africa and Socotra island with heavy bills and, in one species, vivid yellow wing patches.

children.name: Euphonia
children.description: Euphonias — vivid Neotropical finches now placed in Fringillidae by genomic data. Males are typically deep blue-black above with vivid yellow underparts. Specialists on mistletoe berries, they have evolved rapid gut passage to excrete seeds before toxins are absorbed, making them critical mistletoe dispersers in Neotropical forests.

children.name: Euphonia fulvicrissa
children.description: The fulvous-vented euphonia is a species of bird in the family Fringillidae, the finches and euphonias. It is found in Colombia, Ecuador, and Panama.

children.name: Chlorophonia
children.description: Chlorophonias — vivid emerald-green Neotropical finches closely related to euphonias, now classified within Fringillidae. Males are brilliant green with yellow or blue highlights; females predominantly olive. Chlorophonias inhabit montane forests from Mexico to northern South America.
